Family Health

Urinary incontinence in women: types and treatment

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Urinary incontinence means urine leaks when you do not intend it to. It can affect younger women as well as older women, and the impact may reach beyond wet clothing to exercise, sleep, work and intimacy. Help starts with identifying the pattern and any contributing condition. A treatment that helps sudden urgency may do little for leakage during a cough, and an emptying problem needs a different approach again.

Stress, urgency and mixed leakage

Stress incontinence is leakage when pressure rises during coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting or exercise. Here, stress refers to physical pressure rather than emotional stress. Support around the urethra and the ability of its outlet to remain closed can be involved. Leakage is a symptom to discuss, not a measure of how fit or disciplined you are.

Urgency incontinence accompanies a sudden need to urinate that is difficult to postpone. Triggers can include running water or arriving near a toilet. Overactive bladder describes urgency, often with frequency or night-time visits, and can occur without leakage. Mixed incontinence combines stress and urgency leakage; tell the clinician which part bothers you most rather than expecting one treatment to solve both.

Other patterns change the next step

Overflow leakage happens when the bladder does not empty adequately. Dribbling, a weak stream or frequent small amounts may be clues, but symptoms alone cannot measure what remains. Functional incontinence describes difficulty reaching or using a toilet because of mobility, clothing, communication or thinking-related barriers. Improving access and assistance may matter more than adding a bladder medicine.

Continuous or near-continuous leakage also needs assessment. Possible explanations include a structural difference, nerve injury or an abnormal connection such as a fistula between the bladder and vagina. Do not label persistent wetness as weak muscles without checking its origin. The existing guide explains emptying problems in more detail: https://bemamas.com/family-health/urinary-retention-causes-and-diagnosis/

Look for contributing conditions

Urinary leakage is more common in women than in men. Pregnancy, childbirth, pelvic surgery, menopause-related changes, persistent coughing, constipation, diabetes and neurological conditions can be relevant. Higher body weight may increase risk, but it cannot explain an individual's symptoms by itself. Pelvic organ prolapse may coexist with or contribute to urinary symptoms; leakage does not inevitably cause prolapse.

An infection or a change in medicine can produce a new problem or worsen an existing one. Diuretics increase urine production, while other medicines can affect alertness, bladder contraction or emptying. Bring prescriptions and nonprescription products to the review. Do not stop an important medicine on your own, and do not dismiss new symptoms as an unavoidable part of ageing.

Assessment begins with the pattern

A short bladder diary can make the appointment more useful. For about three days, record drinks, toilet visits, leaks, urgent sensations and what you were doing at the time. Include ordinary working and leisure activities if possible. Mention pain, blood, repeated infections, difficulty emptying, bowel symptoms, pregnancy plans and previous pelvic procedures.

Assessment may include urine testing, a pelvic examination with consent, and a cough test to observe stress leakage. A post-void bladder scan is useful when incomplete emptying or recurrent infection is a concern. Blood tests answer selected questions. Urodynamics, cystoscopy and detailed imaging are not a compulsory first-visit package; they are chosen for uncertainty, other findings or particular treatment decisions. Ask how each result would change care.

Practical changes should support daily life

Consider whether caffeine, large drinks at particular times or constipation worsen symptoms. Agree on an appropriate fluid pattern instead of deliberately dehydrating yourself. Weight management, if relevant and wanted, and support to stop smoking can be part of care. A persistent cough deserves attention too. Changes should be manageable rather than a reason to abandon exercise or social activities.

Make toilets easier to reach, use clothing that is manageable, and arrange assistance if needed. Absorbent continence products can help you stay active while assessment or treatment proceeds. Change wet products regularly and ask a continence nurse about suitable cleansing and skin protection if irritation develops. Products contain leakage; they do not establish its cause or mean that treatment is no longer worth discussing.

Pelvic-floor training needs the right target

Supervised pelvic-floor muscle training is commonly offered for stress or mixed incontinence, usually over at least three months before assessing the full response. A clinician or pelvic-health physiotherapist checks technique and adapts practice to your ability. Learning contraction, coordination and complete release is more useful than repeatedly squeezing as hard as possible.

Some people have excessive muscle tension as well as poor function. Pain or increasing difficulty emptying during exercises is a reason to review the plan, not intensify it. Training is not a universal cure for every leakage pattern. For more on muscle tension and weakness, see https://bemamas.com/family-health/pelvic-floor-dysfunction/ or, if you have recently given birth, https://bemamas.com/newborn/pelvic-floor-recovery-after-birth/

Bladder training is different from muscle training

For urgency or mixed leakage, bladder training uses an agreed plan to improve control of urgency and gradually adjust the interval between visits. A course often lasts at least six weeks. Your diary and comfort guide the starting point. The aim is not to endure escalating pain, ignore a full bladder that cannot empty, or meet an arbitrary two-hour target immediately.

Timed or prompted toilet visits may instead suit someone who needs help recognising or acting on the need to go. Double voiding (trying again after a brief pause) is sometimes advised for selected emptying problems, but it does not replace assessment of retained urine. Ask which approach is intended for you and what symptoms should trigger a review.

Medicines mainly address selected symptoms

Antimuscarinic medicines and beta-3 agonists can be options for urgency or overactive-bladder symptoms. Antimuscarinics may cause dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision or emptying difficulty. Their cumulative effects on cognition deserve discussion, particularly in older people or those with existing cognitive problems. Mirabegron requires blood-pressure assessment and monitoring and is unsuitable with severe uncontrolled hypertension; precautions vary between medicines.

Vaginal oestrogen may help when urinary symptoms occur with menopause-related genital or urinary changes. It is different from starting systemic hormone therapy to treat leakage. Duloxetine is sometimes considered for stress incontinence when appropriate, depending on local availability, other options and adverse effects. Arrange a review of benefit and tolerability. Pregnancy, planned conception and breastfeeding need an individual medicine review; do not borrow tablets or stop prescribed treatment abruptly.

Devices and drainage serve different purposes

An appropriately fitted continence pessary sits in the vagina and provides support that may reduce stress leakage. It is not a catheter, an implant or an urgency medicine. Ask about fitting, removal or cleaning, follow-up, and what to do about discomfort, bleeding or difficulty urinating. The appropriate device depends on your anatomy, symptoms and preferences.

A catheter drains urine and may be needed when emptying is inadequate, or for other specifically assessed needs. Intermittent and indwelling catheters have different arrangements and require teaching and follow-up. Catheters can cause infection and other problems, so they are not the automatic solution to ordinary leakage. Do not insert one yourself without the training and plan provided by your care team.

Procedures for stress leakage need a separate decision

Options can include urethral bulking injections, colposuspension or a sling procedure. Bulking aims to improve urethral closure and may need repeating; its effect is generally less durable or less effective than some operations. Colposuspension supports the bladder-neck region. A sling may use your own tissue or, where available and appropriate, synthetic mesh. These are different procedures, not interchangeable names for one operation.

Mesh is a permanent implant and can have complications including exposure, pain and urinary or sexual problems; complete removal may be difficult. Other operations also have risks, including difficult emptying. Ask about alternatives, likely benefit, repeat procedures and follow-up. An artificial urinary sphincter is uncommon in women and reserved for selected complex cases. Future pregnancy can affect results and should be discussed before surgery.

Procedures for urgency target bladder signalling

Bladder injections of botulinum toxin can reduce overactivity in selected patients. The effect wears off and treatment may be repeated. Discuss infection and retention risks, including whether you could manage intermittent catheterisation if needed. These injections have a different target from urethral bulking for stress leakage.

Tibial nerve stimulation and sacral neuromodulation are other specialist options. One involves stimulation through a nerve near the ankle; the other may use an implanted system after assessment or a trial. Visit commitments, repeat treatment, device maintenance and possible further procedures matter. More extensive surgery is uncommon. Choose with the team according to your symptoms, health and preferences rather than assuming everyone must follow an identical ladder.

Review progress and recognise warning signs

Agree on a goal such as fewer leaks during walks or fewer urgent interruptions, and a date to review it. Improvement may mean better control rather than complete dryness. If treatment does not help, revisit the diagnosis, technique, adverse effects and alternatives. Continued symptoms are not a personal failure and do not automatically mean surgery is required.

Sudden inability to pass urine needs emergency assessment. New bladder or bowel changes with back or leg symptoms or numbness around the genitals or buttocks also need emergency help. Seek prompt care for visible blood, fever, painful urination or significant new pelvic or flank pain. During pregnancy, a gush or continuing watery trickle may be leaking waters: contact maternity care urgently rather than assuming it is urine.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Identify the dominant leakage pattern and check for conditions that change the treatment pathway.

Discuss what each option targets, its likely benefits and harms, and how progress will be reviewed.

Guidelines and local availability differ; choices should reflect individual health, pregnancy plans and preferences.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to organise symptom patterns and appointment questions. It cannot measure residual urine, diagnose a fistula or select a medicine, device or operation for you.

When to seek help

Sudden inability to urinate, or new bladder/bowel changes with concerning back, leg or saddle-sensation symptoms, needs emergency assessment. Blood, fever or significant new urinary pain needs prompt care. Possible leaking waters during pregnancy needs urgent maternity advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Describe when leakage happens and whether emptying is difficult; different patterns need different care.
  • A diary and targeted assessment usually come before advanced tests or procedures.
  • Pelvic-floor training and bladder training have different purposes and should be tailored.
  • Medicines, pessaries, injections and operations need discussion of benefits, limits and monitoring.
  • Practical support and treatment can improve daily life, while new urgent symptoms require prompt assessment.

Frequently asked questions

What does urinary incontinence mean?

It means unintended urine leakage. It can occur with coughing or exercise, with urgency, because the bladder does not empty properly, or when reaching a toilet is difficult. Describing the pattern helps guide assessment.

Can urinary incontinence in women be treated?

Often it can improve substantially, and some causes can be corrected. Results depend on the type and contributing conditions. Treatment may combine practical support, tailored training, medicines or procedures; complete dryness is not guaranteed.

What are the symptoms of stress incontinence?

Urine leaks during a cough, sneeze, laugh, lift or other activity that increases pressure. The word stress means physical pressure here. A clinician can check whether this is the main pattern or whether urgency and emptying problems also occur.

What is the best treatment?

There is no single best treatment for every type. Supervised muscle training often helps stress or mixed leakage; bladder training addresses urgency. An emptying problem, functional barrier or continuous leak may require another approach.

Should I drink less to stop leaking?

Do not restrict fluids to the point of dehydration. Review the amount, timing and caffeine content with your clinician, taking account of other health needs. A diary helps identify useful adjustments.

Will I need every bladder test?

No. Urine tests, examination and selected residual measurements guide further decisions. Urodynamics, cystoscopy and scans answer particular questions rather than being mandatory for everyone.

Are all slings made from mesh?

No. Some use a person's own tissue; synthetic mesh is another option in selected settings. Ask exactly which procedure and material are proposed, including alternatives and long-term risks.

What if I am pregnant or planning another pregnancy?

Tell the team before choosing medicines or surgery. Treatment and timing need individual discussion, and pregnancy may affect an operation's result. Possible leaking waters needs urgent maternity advice, even if you have leaked urine before.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
